svg.title: KLN 90B simulation: GPS, RAIM and GPS failures
svg.text: True vs. measured position · filter & Doppler · RAIM & messages · faulty satellite · jamming · spoofing
What the simulation models, what the pilot sees, and how to tell the failures apart
Where the aircraft is ≠ where the unit thinks it is
The simulator knows the true position. The KLN navigates on a measured one, as a real receiver does.
MEASURED position: what the unit navigates on
error ellipse: ≈ 10–20 m with a good sky
Every page shows the measured position; it
also goes to the GPS SimVars, so the
Every satellite range carries two errors:
Slow ranging error σ 4.9 m: orbit, clock, atmosphere.
Receiver noise σ 1 m, new every second.
× the geometry (DOP) turns range errors into a position error:
STA 2 shows the estimate: EPE = 2 × HDOP × 5 m. Three satellites + altitude: far more error than eight.
Doppler and the filter: smooth position, instant speed
Ranges give the position, the carrier’s Doppler shift gives the velocity. A Kalman filter blends the two.
The satellite’s own motion is known from its orbit data and removed;
what is left is your velocity. 1 m/s ≈ 5 Hz at L1 (19 cm). The noise
The Kalman filter (one per axis: north and east)

text.tspan: A satellite joins → the measured position steps
A turn → no lag in speed and track

svg.text: The Doppler velocity follows the truth within one second, so a maneuver has no lag, while a jump in the measured
position is smoothed. The slow satellite error passes through, as on a real receiver. A new fix, a power cycle, a slew
or a teleport restart the filter; a pause holds every output.
Signal strength and the lock rule
Each satellite has its own SNR. One rule decides whether the receiver keeps or finds it, whatever the cause.
SNR depends on the satellite’s height above the antenna
Each satellite scatters around the curve (its block, a slow fade, the estimate’s jitter). Bank and pitch tilt
the antenna: satellites on the low-wing side lose signal.
lost: kept in its channel, searched
One rule for every cause: bank, fade, a jammer, a spoofer. The 5 dB gap stops a satellite flickering.
Getting a fix: the STATE on STA 1
A fix needs 4 satellites, or 3 + the altitude input, and an error estimate within 3.8 NM.

poor for RAIM at this phase’s
Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring. Two questions: is a check possible, and does a range lie?
At least 5 measurements: the altitude input counts as one.

The GPS messages and when the pilot sees them
Shown on the MSG page; the MSG prompt flashes for a new one. Delays count GPS time.
The fix is lost (after a fix since power-on).
NAV flag; STA 1 goes to ACQ.

En route or ARM: the geometry fails the alert limit (comes
Approach active: no RAIM for 0.3 NM.
RAIM is available and the residual test fails: a faulty
satellite, a spoofer, the altitude disagreeing.
Integrity warning; no ACTV; in APR the NAV flag.
The approach gate refused ACTV: no RAIM now, or none
predicted at the FAF or the MAP.
Approach active and integrity lost: the NAV flag is up.
GPS APR leaves the approach mode: nav for the
GPS time differs from the unit’s clock by more than 10
Clock corrected. A spoofer moves it by hours!
The first fix is more than 2 NM from the stored position.
With a failed antenna or receiver STA 1 shows FAILR and its hardware message names the cause; the messages above stay silent. Colors: red = navigation is affected, amber =
A satellite clock jumps. The satellite is not flagged unhealthy yet, so it is used and its range is wrong.
Pulled by the bias through the geometry:
the error can be larger than the bias.
Ground speed and track stay right: a
The bias ramps up, RAIM catches it
RAIM POSITION ERROR (if RAIM is available)
Never flagged unhealthy: this is the hour before the control segment notices.
En route the navigation stays valid. ACTV is refused; in approach active the NAV
flag and PRESS GPS APR FOR NAV.
The unit detects but cannot exclude: the message stays while the satellite is
used. With only 4 measurements nothing is detected.
When the satellite sets, the error goes. After 120 s out of the solution another
STA 1 looks perfectly normal: the faulty satellite has a healthy SNR.
A transmitter on the ground raises the noise floor. Every satellite loses the same number of dB: the weakest go first.
All lost: NAV flag, STA 1 ACQ
Jet at FL350 (a test flight of the simulation): the weakest satellite goes about 121 NM out, the weak ones by 74 NM, the strong ones only within 10 NM. The jammer’s power is drawn so that the first
loss comes 100 to 600 NM out at FL350; nearer the ground it takes them sooner.
What the pilot sees, and the way back
No message of its own: the EPE grows, then RAIM NOT AVAILABLE (only if RAIM is
gone for more than 10 s before the fix), then SATELLITE COVERAGE INADEQUATE FOR
STA 1: the SNRs fall together; lost satellites read *xx 00; with everything gone
Turning toward the jammer makes it worse (antenna gain); banking away helps.
No fix for 5 minutes: INIT, a sky search that keeps the position and the clock.
Away from the jammer or below its horizon: satellites return at SNR 35; the fix
about 40 s after four are back.
A transmitter broadcasts fake satellites: the sky of a receiver standing still at a false place, at a false time.
the unit shows: parked here, GS 0
dashed ring: the spoofer’s radio horizon,
capture starts there (≈ 240 NM at FL350)
The false place is a real airport
with a hard runway of 1500 m or more.
How the fakes overpower the real satellites
distance to the spoofer (NM), flying toward it →
The fake signals raise the noise floor and drown the real satellites. They also jam each other, so
eight fakes level off at an SNR of about 51: a flat, high column on STA 1, the same at every
A searching channel locks the stronger of a PRN’s two signals, if it is 35 or more.
A tracked signal is kept until it falls below 30: real satellites can return while
A fake takes an empty, lost or searching channel, never one that tracks.
Shared PRNs decide how fast the capture is
PRNs up in the believed sky
PRNs up in the fake sky
shared: the receiver searches these anyway
Shift ≈ 6 h: about a third shared →
Shift ≈ 12 h: almost none → no fix; after
5 min a sky search (INIT) → captured after
Position wanders by several to tens of NM; GS and
track wrong; fixes come and go.
RAIM POSITION ERROR, but none with only 4
At jet speed the band can be crossed with no mixed
For as long as it is captured, while RAIM is available. On
the ground it stays silent if the false airport is within
about 500 ft of the field’s elevation.
every row tells the same lie → residual 0
No RAIM message at all. False position, GS 0, a normal
SYSTEM TIME UPDATED TO GPS TIME when the clock jumps
Flying out: the fakes fall below 30 and are lost. The unit then searches from its false belief, which is far off: after 5 minutes it searches the whole sky, and the true position returns
STA 1 tells you what is wrong
Same page, six situations. Look at the SNR column, the elevations and the state.
+ RAIM POSITION ERROR → faulty satellite: cross-check with VOR/DME; no GPS approach. It ends
→ just geometry: check the EPE on STA 2 and RAIM on STA 5; wait for satellites to rise.
→ jamming: fly by VOR/DME; turn away, descend below the jammer’s horizon.
Equal SNRs at any elevation, GS 0, clock
→ spoofing: trust neither position nor time; leave or descend; expect a slow recovery.
The way out: get below the transmitter’s horizon
Satellites are overhead, the jammer or spoofer is on the ground. Earth’s curvature can hide the transmitter, never the sky.
line of sight to the transmitter
Below the dashed line: the shadow. Just under it a diffraction band
(2 dB per NM), so the transmitter fades in and out, not at a hard edge.
(curvature exaggerated; the earth is smooth: terrain does not mask a transmitter)
Radio horizon of a 100 ft mast and the aircraft:
distance = 1.23 × (√100 + √h) NM, h in feet above ground
Example: a transmitter 80 NM away is hidden below about 3,000 ft AGL; go a little lower for the
diffraction band. One 20 NM away is hidden only on the ground.
Attitude matters too, and the way back
Overhead, the antenna’s underside shields: a high aircraft can overfly a weak
Climbing back brings it back: the transmitter stays where it is.
Jamming: satellites return at SNR 35; the fix about 40 s after four are back.
Spoofing: the unit starts from its false belief: 5 to 15 minutes, then SYSTEM TIME
